If `x` doesn't have an `attrs` attribute (e.g., it's a scalar), `getattr` returns the default value `{}` (an empty dictionary). This ensures that attributes are either taken from `x` or are empty, preventing the unintended inheritance of attributes from `cond` as pointed out by the reviewer.

I'm wondering why `wsgi.py` is placed before `app.py`?

`wsgi.py` is usually used for production environment. In this case, we don't have to use flask cli to create the server. On the other hand, `app.py` is what we used for development, it is better to put `app.py` before `wsgi.py`.

I guess many custom CLI functions are also used in production. Either way, if it's a `wsgi.py` I'd expect it to be used only when running the WSGI app - not necessarily for other CLI functionality.

Anyway, if people do use CLI commands in production I think they should strongly consider adding their own CLI that knows how to instantiate the app instead of using the generic `flask` command...

@lepture I don't see the use of `wsgi.py` and `app.py` as being different for production or development. Regardless of the one you use, it's going to be part of your project, so it will be present in both environments. I used very simple logic to decide that `wsgi.py` should be first:

- If you have neither `app.py` nor `wsgi.py` in your project, it does not matter which one you check first.
- If you have only one of `app.py` and `wsgi.py` in your project, it also does not matter.
- If you have both `app.py` and `wsgi.py` in your project, I think it would be wrong to ignore `wsgi.py` in favor of `app.py`, since I see no other function for a `wsgi.py` file than to be the module that defines the app.

@ThiefMaster I don't follow some of your statements:

> Either way, if it's a `wsgi.py` I'd expect it to be used only when running the WSGI app - not necessarily for other CLI functionality.

The app is going to be needed when running most CLI commands. Maybe there are some cases in which you want to define custom commands that do not require the app, but that is not going to be the general case. In fact, the CLI defaults to creating an app context for your command, so right there you can see that you have to have the app.

> Anyway, if people do use CLI commands in production

It's not just people. Extensions define their own commands as well. My Flask-Migrate extension adds a bunch of commands under `flask db` that are used in production and development.

>  I think they should strongly consider adding their own CLI

That would be tricky for commands added by extensions. But even for the app's own custom commands, what's the benefit of using a separate CLI? There is nothing wrong with that idea if that's what you prefer, but I don't see how that would be a recommendation to be made in the general case.

>  that knows how to instantiate the app instead of using the generic flask command...

Well, the flask command has to know how to instantiate the app anyway, so why invent a different method for custom commands? It guess you are thinking that the flask command does not have a place in production, but in any case, why would you want to create the app in a different way between dev and prod? Normally the app is the same, and you just change the configuration.

> The app is going to be needed when running most CLI commands.

Sure, I just meant that you don't use the WSGI part of Flask in the CLI, so `wsgi.py` is not *that* obvious there

> My Flask-Migrate extension adds a bunch of commands under flask db that are used in production and development.
> That would be tricky for commands added by extensions

When using `FlaskGroup` for the CLI command defined via entry points show up in a custom CLI too

> but in any case, why would you want to create the app in a different way between dev and prod

I wouldn't - I'd use the custom command for both dev and prod. My point was just that if your app does use more advanced CLI commands than just `run` and `shell` it might be a good point to add a custom CLI, especially considering that it doesn't take more than a few lines of code.

> If you have both app.py and wsgi.py in your project, I think it would be wrong to ignore wsgi.py in favor of app.py, since I see no other function for a wsgi.py file than to be the module that defines the app.

Yes. I always have both `app.py` and `wsgi.py` in my project. The `wsgi.py` as I understand, is designed to be a pure wsgi application, which would contain just a few lines of code. Something as simple as:

```python
from your_project import create_app
app = create_app()
```

The `wsgi.py` file could be used by gunicorn/uwsgi etc. The idea comes from Django.

Like Django, I take `app.py` as the `manage.py`, which could contain a lot of custom commands, e.g. `initdb`, `createuser`.

> Sure, I just meant that you don't use the WSGI part of Flask in the CLI, so wsgi.py is not that obvious there

Fair enough. I see what you meant now. I don't know how to separate the WSGI and non-WSGI uses of the app instance. Using `wsgi.py` is totally clear in my mind as a way to tell a web server what is the application, and you need to do this whether you use `flask run`, gunicorn or uwsgi. The `flask shell` or `flask something-else` cases are strange, I agree.
